paragraph.text: PQC Detection and Remediation by Language and Compute

Outbound TLS becomes post-quantum (PQ) only when the client's TLS library offers the hybrid group X25519MLKEM768 in TLS 1.3. Whether it does depends on the language runtime and its crypto library, not on the compute type. Compute type decides two other things: how you can see non-PQ connections, and how the fix ships.
differs by compute type. Lambda and Fargate cannot be packet-mirrored, so they rely on AWS logs and app-side telemetry. Containers on EC2 can also use passive sensors.
differs by language and version. Some need only a config file, some a Java agent or library shim, and some a runtime or toolchain upgrade.

Inbound: front doors and TLS 1.3 enforcement

Inbound connections become PQ when the front door's TLS policy offers ML-KEM and the caller supports it. Allow TLS 1.2 and 1.3 first, measure, then move each endpoint to TLS 1.3 only once its TLS 1.2 traffic reaches zero. TLS negotiation already picks 1.3 when both sides support it, and TLS 1.3's downgrade protection stops an attacker forcing 1.2.

Rollout through build, package and release
Every change, including configuration, ships as a release here. So the fix lives in the shared build template, and each workload picks it up on its next release with no per-service code edits.

embed.caption: rollout loop · 4 steps, repeated per release cycle

paragraph.text: The release step is the only one that changes a workload; the others are automation around it.
The posture inventory sorts each workload into a matrix row and records the gap.
A bot opens a pull request in each repo that bumps the shared module or template. The template ships the right files under
(config file, agent jar or shim) and sets the matching variable. It leaves a workload's own
alone and flags it for review. Bundling into the package avoids Lambda's 5-layer limit.

The normal pipeline builds, packages and releases. A guardrail (cfn-guard, OPA/conftest or a CloudFormation Hook) warns, then later fails, on Lambda and task definitions missing the PQ settings, and on non-PQ ELB policies.
Observed signals confirm the workload's connections moved to PQ; shipping isn't proof. CLM tracks each workload as a campaign item.

Dormant workloads with no release coming: rank them by observed classical traffic. One making no classical outbound TLS doesn't need forcing; the rest get a no-op rebuild and release. Runtimes past AWS's block-update date can't be changed at all, so schedule those first.
